clinician.trajectory_summary: A man in his 70s presented with acute 3-day brainstem syndrome (gait disturbance, left hemiparaesthesia, dysarthria, dysphagia) and MRI showing brainstem and left caudate nucleus lesions initially suspected to be tumor. Key diagnostic workup revealed neuroinflammatory rather than neoplastic features: MRI showed hyperintense DWI/ADC signal without gadolinium enhancement and spectroscopy indicating elevated choline with preserved NAA; CSF was acellular with negative cytology and oligoclonal bands; serum studies were negative for cancer markers (CEA, CA19-9, soluble IL-2 receptor) and autoimmune antibodies (AQP4, MOG, ANA, ANCA, RF). The patient had historical uveitis with blindness (major Behçet's criterion) and was HLA-B51 positive, though he lacked active mucocutaneous lesions (no oral/genital ulcers, no skin rash) and had negative pathergy on examination. Based on acute brainstem lesion, MRI findings, and HLA-B51 positivity, he was treated with intravenous methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by oral corticosteroids and colchicine. Two-month follow-up demonstrated radiological reduction of brain lesions and clinical amelioration with only minor residual left hemiparesis and gait disturbance. While he did not meet International Study Group Criteria for Behçet's disease (lacking documented recurrent oral ulcers), he fulfilled criteria for probable neuro-Behçet's disease per International consensus recommendation criteria.
